intro: Two powerful forces reshaped martial arts in the twentieth century: the movie camera and the television contract. Films from Shanghai, Tokyo, Hong Kong and Hollywood gave audiences heroes, schools and styles. Some of those schools were real, with founders and records. Others were written for a script and then painted on the doors of real gyms.

Mixed martial arts grew from a different kind of screen. In 1993 a television company staged an eight-man tournament in Denver and sold it on pay-per-view. Within a few years, politicians called for bans. The sport survived by accepting rule books and licenses from state athletic commissions, the same offices that had overseen boxing since 1920.

In this unit you will read films as historical sources. You will learn to separate a studio's advertising from the record, and a legend from a dated document. You will also trace how a new league borrowed rooms from wrestling, boxing, judo and Muay Thai, and how laws in states like New Jersey, New York and Illinois shaped it.
bigQuestion: Who gets to name a style or run a sport: the people who film it, the people who sell it, or the people who regulate it?

title: Film and the New League

chapters.title: Invented Style
chapters.bigQuestion: When a film invents a style, who decides what a school may call itself afterward?

story.title: A Name From the Screen
story.kicker: A new student asks a karate teacher for a style that was written for a script.
paragraphs: It is a Saturday morning at a small karate school in a suburban strip mall. A tenth grader comes in with a parent to sign up. The teacher asks what the student hopes to learn. The student answers with one word: Miyagi-do. The student has watched every season of the streaming series Cobra Kai, which began in 2018.

The teacher smiles and points to a framed photograph near the front desk. It shows Miyagi Chōjun, a real teacher from Naha, Okinawa, who lived from 1888 to 1953. His school is called Gōjū-ryū. The teacher explains that screenwriters for the 1984 film The Karate Kid gave their fictional teacher the name Miyagi. Miyagi-do is a name made for that story.

The student looks surprised but stays curious. The parent asks a practical question. Are there real schools that call themselves Miyagi-do now? The teacher says some gyms have borrowed names from films. Some people also sell shirts and classes under those names. A name on a door does not prove a long history behind it.

This small conversation holds a large question. Films from Shanghai, Tokyo, Hong Kong and Hollywood have named styles for more than ninety years. Some names came from real schools. Others were made up by writers and directors. Historians sort them by asking a simple question: what records exist before the film?
story.think: Why might a teacher keep a photograph of a real founder near the front desk of a school?

lessons.title: The Red Lotus Serial
lessons.mainIdea: Shanghai studios turned wuxia novels into film serials in the late 1920s, and the Nationalist government's censors soon banned them.
reading: In the 1920s, Chinese newspapers and magazines printed long adventure stories in parts. One of the most famous was by Xiang Kairan, who wrote under the pen name Pingjiang Buxiaosheng. His novel told of heroes of the *jianghu*, a word meaning rivers and lakes. In these stories, the jianghu is a world of wandering fighters outside the law.

In 1928 the Mingxing Film Company in Shanghai released The Burning of the Red Lotus Temple. It was based on part of Xiang's novel and directed by Zhang Shichuan. Audiences lined up, so the studio made sequel after sequel. A *serial* is a film story released in many parts over time. Other Shanghai studios rushed out their own sword-hero films.

The Nationalist government, led by the Guomindang party, set up film censors around this time. In the early 1930s the censors banned the Red Lotus films and many like them. Officials said the films spread superstition, since heroes flew and used magic. The ban pushed this kind of filmmaking out of Shanghai. Much of it later grew again in Hong Kong. *Censorship* shaped where martial arts films were made.

words.d: "rivers and lakes"; in Chinese adventure fiction, the world of wandering fighters outside the law
a film or story released in many parts, one after another
a government or other authority stopping or cutting books, films or speech it does not approve

look.title: Two Kinds of Record
look.text: Record A: a 1928 newspaper advertisement for The Burning of the Red Lotus Temple, a new film from the Mingxing company in Shanghai. Record B: a government notice from the early 1930s listing films that may no longer be shown because they spread superstition.
look.prompt: What does each record tell a historian about who had power over films in Shanghai at the time?

check.q: What does the Chinese word jianghu mean in adventure fiction?
choices: Rivers and lakes, the world of wandering fighters
A training hall in a temple
A rank given by a school
check.why: Jianghu means rivers and lakes; in fiction it names the world of wandering heroes.

check.q: Which company released The Burning of the Red Lotus Temple in 1928?
check.why: The Mingxing Film Company in Shanghai made the 1928 film and its sequels.

check.q: Why did Nationalist censors ban the Red Lotus films in the early 1930s?
choices: They were filmed in Hong Kong
check.why: Censors objected to flying heroes and magic, calling it superstition.

lessons.title: Opera Schools and Screen Fights
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hong Kong film fighters first trained in Peking opera schools, so screen fights grew out of stage performance.
reading: *Peking opera* is a Chinese stage art that joins singing, acting, music and acrobatics. It took shape in Beijing in the late 1700s and 1800s. Some roles include staged battles with swords and spears. Performers learned these scenes as part of theater, not as fighting for a contest.

In Hong Kong in the 1960s, Yu Jim-yuen ran a Peking opera school called the China Drama Academy. Children lived at the school and trained for many hours each day. A group of its students performed together as the Seven Little Fortunes. Jackie Chan, Sammo Hung and Yuen Biao all trained there as boys.

When live opera lost audiences, many of these performers found work in film. They became actors, *stunt* performers and fight designers. Their scenes came from *choreography*, planned movement worked out ahead of time. This history explains why Hong Kong screen fights look like dance and acrobatics. The style on screen came from a theater tradition, not from a single fighting school.

words.d: a Chinese stage art that joins singing, acting, music and acrobatics, formed in Beijing
a difficult or dangerous action done for a film, often by a trained performer
movement planned and practiced ahead of time for a performance

look.title: Stage or Contest?
look.text: Picture two photographs from Hong Kong in the 1960s. In one, children in costume stand in a row on a theater stage, holding painted wooden spears. In the other, two boxers stand in a ring with a referee between them and a judge at a table.
look.prompt: Which photograph shows a planned performance, and which shows a contest with a winner? What clues tell you?

check.q: What kind of school did Yu Jim-yuen run in Hong Kong?
check.why: Yu Jim-yuen ran the China Drama Academy, a Peking opera school.

check.q: Which actors trained at the China Drama Academy?
choices: Jackie Chan, Sammo Hung and Yuen Biao
check.why: Jackie Chan, Sammo Hung and Yuen Biao were among its students.

check.q: What is choreography?
choices: Movement planned and practiced ahead of time
check.why: Choreography means planned movement, which is how stage and film fights are made.

lessons.title: Kurosawa's Judo Story
lessons.mainIdea: Kurosawa Akira's first film, Sanshiro Sugata (1943), turned the early Kodokan into a screen legend during wartime.
reading: In 1942 the writer Tomita Tsuneo published a novel called Sanshiro Sugata. His father, Tomita Tsunejirō, had been one of Kanō Jigorō's first students at the Kodokan in Tokyo. The novel follows a young judo student in the 1880s. Many readers think the hero was loosely based on Saigō Shirō, a famous early Kodokan student.

In 1943 the director Kurosawa Akira made the novel into his first film. It was released by the Toho studio in the middle of World War II. The film shows judo rising against older jujutsu schools. It is a *dramatization*, a story built on history with invented scenes and speeches. Kurosawa later became one of the best-known directors in the world.

Japan's wartime government watched films closely. Censors later cut scenes from Sanshiro Sugata, and some of the original footage is still lost. The film shows how the early years of a real institution, the *Kodokan*, became a legend on screen. A historian compares the film with Kodokan records and Kanō's own writings to see which parts are documented.

words.d: a story for stage or screen built on real history but with invented scenes and speeches
the judo school Kanō Jigorō founded in Tokyo in 1882; still judo's headquarters
a large Japanese film studio founded in the 1930s

look.title: A Novel Behind a Film
look.text: Tomita Tsuneo's novel follows a young man from the countryside who joins a new judo hall in Tokyo in the 1880s and faces rivals from older jujutsu schools.
look.cite: Tomita Tsuneo, Sanshiro Sugata (novel), 1942; filmed by Kurosawa Akira, Toho, 1943
look.prompt: Which parts of this summary could a historian check against Kodokan records, and which parts belong to the novelist?

check.q: What was Sanshiro Sugata (1943) in Kurosawa Akira's career?
choices: A film made in Hong Kong
check.why: Sanshiro Sugata was Kurosawa's first film as a director, released by Toho in 1943.

check.q: How was the novelist Tomita Tsuneo connected to the Kodokan?
choices: His father was one of Kanō Jigorō's first students
check.why: Tomita Tsunejirō, the novelist's father, was among Kanō's first Kodokan students.

check.q: What is a dramatization?
choices: A story built on history with invented scenes
A government record of a match
A rule book for a sport
check.why: A dramatization uses real history but adds invented scenes and speeches, as Sanshiro Sugata does.

lessons.title: Lau Kar-leung's Family Line
lessons.mainIdea: Director Lau Kar-leung came from a real Hung Ga lineage, yet his Shaolin films still mixed tradition with invention.
reading: Lau Kar-leung lived from 1934 to 2013. He grew up in a family that taught Hung Ga, a southern Chinese style. His father, Lau Charn, had studied with Lam Sai-wing. Lam Sai-wing had been a student of Wong Fei-hung. This chain of teachers is a *lineage*, a line passed from teacher to student.

Lau began as a fight designer in Hong Kong films and became a director at the Shaw Brothers studio in the 1970s. Hong Kong studios gave this job its own title: *martial arts director*. The martial arts director planned every fight scene. Lau's knowledge of Hung Ga shaped how his films showed southern Chinese arts.

In 1978 Lau directed The 36th Chamber of Shaolin, starring Gordon Liu. The hero, San Te, is a figure from Shaolin *folklore*. The film shows him passing through thirty-five training chambers and founding a thirty-sixth. That chamber system belongs to the film's story. The film was a hit across Asia and later in the West, and many viewers took its plot as history.

words.d: a line of teachers and students, each passing a tradition to the next
in Hong Kong film, the person who plans and directs the fight scenes
traditional stories passed on by a community, often without written records

look.title: One Name, Two Kinds of Evidence
look.text: Evidence A: a Hong Kong school's list of teachers, running from Wong Fei-hung to Lam Sai-wing to Lau Charn. Evidence B: a 1978 film in which the monk San Te builds a new training chamber at Shaolin.
look.prompt: Which piece of evidence could a historian check with other records? What would you look for?

check.q: Which style did Lau Kar-leung's family teach?
check.why: Lau's father Lau Charn taught Hung Ga, a southern Chinese style.

check.q: What did a martial arts director do in Hong Kong films?
choices: Planned and directed the fight scenes
check.why: The martial arts director planned every fight scene in a film.

check.q: Which part of The 36th Chamber of Shaolin belongs to the film's story?
choices: The system of thirty-six training chambers
check.why: The chamber system was created for the film; San Te comes from folklore.

lessons.title: Chang Cheh and Screen Schools
lessons.mainIdea: Director Chang Cheh made violent hero films for Shaw Brothers and invented secret schools to drive their plots.
reading: Chang Cheh lived from 1923 to 2002 and was one of Shaw Brothers' leading directors. His 1967 film The One-Armed Swordsman is often described as the first Hong Kong film to earn one million Hong Kong dollars. Its success helped move Hong Kong studios toward tougher male heroes and more fighting on screen.

In 1978 Chang directed Five Deadly Venoms. The plot follows five students of one secret clan. Each student has an animal name, such as Centipede or Scorpion. The clan and its five named methods serve the story. Screenwriters often invent a *secret society* or a lost school because it gives the plot a mystery to solve.

Fans of the film later formed clubs and gave its actors the nickname the Venom Mob. Some viewers searched for the clan as if it were a real school. A careful reader checks for records outside the film. A real school leaves traces such as a founder's name, a place, dated photographs and students who taught others. An *invented style* leaves only the film and what fans built from it.

words.d: a group whose members keep their activities hidden; in films, often an invented school or clan
a fighting style created for a story, with no record outside the film or book
a large Hong Kong film studio that made hundreds of martial arts films

look.title: Traces a School Leaves
look.text: Imagine searching for a style. For Style A, you find a founder's gravestone, a dated photograph of students in 1935, and a teacher list reaching to today. For Style B, you find a 1978 film poster, fan websites and a toy figure.
look.prompt: Which style has records outside a film? What would you still want to check about Style A?

check.q: Which studio did Chang Cheh direct for?
check.why: Chang Cheh was a leading director at Shaw Brothers in Hong Kong.

check.q: What kind of evidence shows that a style has a history outside a film?
choices: A founder's name, a place and dated records
A fan nickname for the actors
check.why: Real schools leave traces like founders, places, dated photographs and students.

check.q: Why do screenwriters often invent a secret school?
choices: Real schools refuse to be filmed
It gives the plot a mystery
check.why: A secret society or lost school gives a story a mystery for heroes to solve.

lessons.title: Yuen Woo-ping Crosses the Pacific
lessons.mainIdea: Hong Kong fight director Yuen Woo-ping carried Hong Kong film methods into Hollywood with The Matrix in 1999.
reading: Yuen Woo-ping was born in 1945. His father, Simon Yuen Siu-tin, was a Peking opera performer and a film actor. In 1978 Yuen directed Drunken Master, starring Jackie Chan as the young Wong Fei-hung. His father played Beggar So, a figure from Cantonese folk stories about Wong's circle. The film mixed comedy with fights and made Jackie Chan a star.

Hong Kong fight directors used *wire work*, hidden cables that lift actors into the air. The cables are erased or hidden in the final film. Wire work goes back to the flying heroes of wuxia films and to stage tricks. It lets a character seem to run up walls or float, which no real fighter does.

In 1999 Warner Bros. released The Matrix, directed by the Wachowskis. Yuen designed its fights and trained the actors for months. He later worked on Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000) and Kill Bill (2003). His career shows how a Hong Kong film *craft* became part of Hollywood action films. The style audiences saw was a film method, not a school.

words.d: a film method using hidden cables to lift actors so they seem to fly or leap
a skilled trade or method, passed on by working with experts
a 1978 Hong Kong comedy film directed by Yuen Woo-ping and starring Jackie Chan

look.title: Films With Yuen Woo-ping's Fight Work
look.cite: Studio release records (Seasonal Film, Warner Bros., Sony Pictures Classics, Miramax)
look.prompt: How many years passed between Yuen's first Hong Kong hits and his first Hollywood film on this list?

check.q: What is wire work in films?
choices: A rank in a film studio
Hidden cables that lift actors into the air
check.why: Wire work uses hidden cables so actors seem to fly or leap.

check.q: Which 1999 Hollywood film did Yuen Woo-ping design fights for?
check.why: Yuen designed the fights for The Matrix, released by Warner Bros. in 1999.

check.q: Who starred in Drunken Master (1978)?
check.why: Jackie Chan played the young Wong Fei-hung in Drunken Master.

lessons.title: Miyagi-do and Cobra Kai
lessons.mainIdea: Miyagi-do and Cobra Kai are dojo names written for The Karate Kid, and they later appeared on real products and gyms.
reading: The Karate Kid (1984) was written by Robert Mark Kamen. The film gives the teacher Mr. Miyagi an Okinawan background. His way of teaching is later called Miyagi-do in the films. The rival school in the story is Cobra Kai. Both are fictional *dojo*, created for the screenplay.

The real Miyagi Chōjun founded Gōjū-ryū karate in Naha, Okinawa, in the early 1900s. The film's character shares his family name, but the story does not claim they are the same person. The Karate Kid became one of the biggest box office hits of 1984. Pat Morita was nominated for an Academy Award for playing Mr. Miyagi.

In 2018 the series Cobra Kai began on YouTube Red, and it moved to Netflix in 2020. The series brought both fictional names back to a new audience. Names from films can be registered as a *trademark*, which means others may not freely sell goods under them. A real school with a long lineage and a brand from a film are different kinds of claims.

words.d: a Japanese word for a training hall
a legally protected name or symbol that only its owner may use to sell goods or services
the written script of a film, with its story, scenes and dialogue

look.title: Two Signs on One Street
look.text: Sign A: "Gōjū-ryū Karate, lineage from Miyagi Chōjun of Naha, Okinawa." Sign B: "Miyagi-do Karate, as seen on screen." Both signs hang above storefronts on the same street.
look.prompt: What is each sign claiming? Which claim can be checked with records older than 1984?

check.q: Who wrote The Karate Kid (1984)?
check.why: Robert Mark Kamen wrote the screenplay for The Karate Kid.

check.q: What did the real Miyagi Chōjun found?
check.why: Miyagi Chōjun of Naha founded Gōjū-ryū; Miyagi-do is a film name.

check.q: What does a trademark do?
choices: It protects a name so only its owner may sell goods under it
check.why: A trademark is a legally protected name or symbol for selling goods or services.

lessons.title: The Ninja Boom
lessons.mainIdea: Historical shinobi served lords in Japan's warring era, but the black-clad ninja of films is largely a stage and screen image.
reading: In Japan's era of civil wars, from the late 1400s to about 1600, lords hired spies and raiders. Records call them *shinobi*. Many came from Iga Province and from the Kōka district of Ōmi Province. After 1600 the Tokugawa government employed Iga men as guards and watchmen in Edo.

Later stories and plays made shinobi into heroes and villains with near-magic powers. Kabuki theater used stagehands dressed all in black, called *kuroko*, who were meant to be ignored. Many historians think this stage custom helped create the popular picture of the ninja in black. Few records from the warring era describe such a costume.

Film carried the image around the world. The James Bond film You Only Live Twice (1967) shot ninja training scenes at Himeji Castle. Cannon Films released Enter the Ninja in 1981, and more ninja films followed. In 1984 Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird published the first Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles comic. Soon American strip malls had schools selling *ninjutsu*, the arts linked to shinobi.

words.d: spies and raiders hired by Japanese lords, especially from the 1400s to about 1600
kabuki stagehands dressed in black, meant to be treated as invisible
a name for the arts linked to the shinobi; used by many modern schools

look.title: Ninjas Reach a World Audience
look.cite: Eon Productions, Cannon Films and Mirage Studios release records
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first Ninja Turtles comic and the first Ninja Turtles film?

check.q: Which two places supplied many historical shinobi?
choices: Iga Province and the Kōka district
check.why: Records link many shinobi to Iga Province and Kōka in Ōmi Province.

check.q: What were kuroko in kabuki theater?
choices: Stagehands in black meant to be ignored
check.why: Kuroko were black-clad stagehands; many historians link them to the ninja image.

check.q: Which 1967 film shot ninja scenes at Himeji Castle?
check.why: The James Bond film You Only Live Twice filmed ninja training at Himeji Castle.

lessons.title: A Kumite Without Records
lessons.mainIdea: Bloodsport (1988) was sold as a true story, but reporters found no records of the secret tournament it showed.
reading: In 1988 Cannon Films released Bloodsport, starring Jean-Claude Van Damme. The film claimed to be based on the life of Frank Dux, an American martial arts teacher. It shows a secret, invitation-only contest in Hong Kong called the *kumite*. In karate, kumite is an ordinary word for sparring with a partner.

Dux said he had won such a tournament in 1975. In 1988 the Los Angeles Times published a report that questioned his claims. Reporters found no records of the tournament and no outside witnesses. A claim backed only by the person who makes it is *unverified*. Dux has defended his account.

Bloodsport still shaped the business of martial arts. Gyms in the late 1980s and 1990s advertised kumite nights and full-contact events. The case shows why historians separate a studio's advertising from the record. A poster that says true story is a marketing claim. *Corroboration*, support from independent sources, is what turns a claim into history.

words.d: a Japanese karate word for sparring with a partner
not yet confirmed by evidence from anyone besides the person who makes the claim
support for a claim from independent sources

look.title: Checking a Poster
look.text: A 1988 movie poster reads: based on a true story. The film shows an underground tournament in Hong Kong. No newspaper from 1975 mentions the event. No official from any sports body is named. The only witness is the man the film is about.
look.prompt: What would you need to find before you called this tournament a historical event?

check.q: What does kumite mean in karate?
check.why: Kumite is an ordinary karate word for sparring; the film made it sound secret.

check.q: Which newspaper questioned Frank Dux's claims in 1988?
check.why: The Los Angeles Times published a 1988 report that questioned the claims.

check.q: What is corroboration?
choices: Support for a claim from independent sources
check.why: Corroboration means independent support, which the Bloodsport tournament lacked.

sections.title: Reading a Film as a Source

lessons.title: The Shaolin Temple, 1982
lessons.mainIdea: The 1982 film The Shaolin Temple retold a Tang dynasty event recorded on a stone stele and drew crowds of visitors to the real monastery.
reading: Shaolin Monastery stands on Mount Song in Henan Province, China. A stone *stele*, a carved stone record, stands there dated 728 CE. It records that Shaolin monks helped Li Shimin, a Tang prince, in a war in 621. In return, the Tang court confirmed the monastery's lands.

In 1982 a Hong Kong company released The Shaolin Temple, filmed in mainland China. Its star was Li Lianjie, known abroad as Jet Li. He had won several national *wushu* titles on the Beijing team. The plot turns the stele's brief record into a story of thirteen heroic monks. Most scenes and characters are invented.

The film filled theaters across China. Visitors began arriving at the real monastery in large numbers. In the following decades, schools opened in the nearby city of Dengfeng and enrolled many thousands of students. A film changed the *economy* of a real place, bringing tourism and new schools.

words.d: an upright carved stone that records an event, law or gift
the Mandarin word for martial arts; also the name of China's modern competitive sport
the way a place makes money, jobs and trade

look.title: The Stone at Shaolin
look.text: A stele at Shaolin Monastery, dated 728, records that monks aided the Tang prince Li Shimin in 621 and that the Tang court afterward confirmed the monastery's land.
look.cite: Shaolin Monastery Stele, 728 CE; discussed in Meir Shahar, The Shaolin Monastery (2008)
look.prompt: What does the stele record, and what did the 1982 film add to it?

check.q: What is a stele?
check.why: A stele is a carved stone; the Shaolin stele of 728 records the monks' help to Li Shimin.

check.q: In what province is Shaolin Monastery?
check.why: Shaolin stands on Mount Song in Henan Province.

check.q: How did The Shaolin Temple (1982) change the real monastery's area?
choices: It brought many visitors and new schools
It moved the monastery to Hong Kong
check.why: After the film, tourists came in large numbers and schools grew in Dengfeng.

lessons.title: What a Film Can Prove
lessons.mainIdea: A film is strong evidence about the time and people who made it, and weak evidence about the past it shows.
reading: Historians treat a film as a *primary source* about its own making. Enter the Dragon (1973) is a good example. Warner Bros. made it with Concord Production, the Hong Kong company Bruce Lee formed with Raymond Chow. The film proves that a Hollywood studio would invest in a Hong Kong star in 1973. It does not prove anything about a real island tournament.

Films also show what audiences wanted. Mighty Morphin Power Rangers began on American television in 1993. Its fight scenes were taken from Toei's Japanese Super Sentai series and joined to new footage shot with American actors. The show tells a historian about global television business in the 1990s. Some martial arts schools of the 1990s advertised classes to the show's young fans.

Careful writers cite a film by title, year, studio and director. They *paraphrase* dialogue, retelling it in their own words, unless they have the exact script. Then they ask three questions. Who made this film, and when? Whom was it made for? What records outside the film agree or disagree? These questions turn a movie into evidence.

chapters.title: MMA as a League
chapters.bigQuestion: How did mixed martial arts turn from a televised experiment into a licensed, regulated league?

story.title: A Stamp on the Bout Sheet
story.kicker: Before anyone enters the cage, a state official signs and stamps a sheet of paper.
paragraphs: It is late afternoon inside an arena outside Chicago. The seats are still empty. In a back hallway, an inspector from the state sits at a folding table with a stack of forms. Each form is a bout sheet. It lists two fighters, their weights, their weight class and the number of rounds.

The inspector checks each fighter's license. A license is a permit from the state that says a person may compete for pay. The inspector also checks for a signed medical form and blood test results. Only then does the inspector sign the sheet and press the agency's stamp on it. Without that stamp, the bout does not happen.

This paperwork is newer than many fans realize. The first Ultimate Fighting Championship, held in Denver in 1993, sold itself as a contest with almost no rules. It had no weight classes and no time limits. Within a few years, politicians called for bans, and several states refused to allow such events at all.

The change came through rule books and government offices. State athletic commissions, first built to oversee boxing, wrote rules for this new sport. Promoters accepted them to win back television and arenas. The stamp on the bout sheet is the sign of that history. It shows that mixed martial arts is a modern league answering to the law.
story.think: Why would a promoter accept strict rules from a state office instead of running events without them?

lessons.title: Pankration at Olympia
lessons.mainIdea: Ancient Greeks held pankration, a contest joining boxing and wrestling, at the Olympic Games from 648 BCE.
reading: The ancient Olympic Games were held at Olympia, in southern Greece. By tradition, *pankration* joined the program in 648 BCE. The name means all strength or all power. It combined parts of boxing and wrestling, two older Olympic events, into one contest.

Pankration had rules and officials. Ancient writers say biting and gouging were forbidden. Referees carried sticks to punish fouls, and vase paintings show them doing it. There were no weight classes. Men and boys competed in separate age groups, and only freeborn Greek males could enter the Olympic events.

Pankration ended with the ancient Games themselves, which faded out by about the late 300s CE. In the 1990s, promoters of mixed martial arts sometimes pointed to pankration as an ancestor. Historians treat that as an *analogy*, a comparison between two things, not a direct line. No teacher or institution links ancient Olympia to a modern cage.

words.d: an ancient Greek Olympic contest that combined boxing and wrestling; first held in 648 BCE by tradition
a comparison showing how two different things are alike in some way
the sanctuary in southern Greece where the ancient Olympic Games were held

lessons.title: Vale Tudo in Brazil
lessons.mainIdea: In Brazil, the Gracie family built an academy and a reputation through open-rules contests called vale tudo.
reading: Mitsuyo Maeda was a Japanese judo expert trained at the Kodokan. He traveled through the Americas in the early 1900s, giving public matches. He settled in Belém, in the Brazilian state of Pará. There, around 1917, a teenager named Carlos Gracie began learning from him.

Carlos Gracie moved to Rio de Janeiro and opened an academy with his brothers in 1925. His younger brother Hélio became the family's best-known competitor. The family's teaching became known as *Brazilian jiu-jitsu*. The family also offered public challenges and took part in open-rules matches. In Portuguese these were called *vale tudo*, which means anything goes.

In October 1951, Hélio Gracie faced the Japanese judo champion Masahiko Kimura at the Maracanã stadium in Rio. Kimura won. The match is still remembered in both Brazil and Japan. Vale tudo shows were a local entertainment in Brazil for decades. They were *precursors*, earlier events that came before a later form, to the league that began in 1993.

Portuguese for anything goes; open-rules fighting contests held in Brazil in the 1900s

lessons.title: Ali and Inoki in Tokyo
lessons.mainIdea: The 1976 bout between Muhammad Ali and Antonio Inoki in Tokyo was an early mixed contest shown around the world.
reading: On June 26, 1976, the boxing champion Muhammad Ali met the Japanese professional wrestler Antonio Inoki. The bout took place at the Nippon Budokan in Tokyo. It was shown on *closed-circuit* television, broadcast to theaters and arenas that sold tickets. The two sides argued over the rules until shortly before the event.

The bout went fifteen rounds and was declared a draw. Many viewers at the time called it dull. Still, it showed that a boxer against a wrestler could draw a world audience. In Japan, Inoki's company and later groups kept staging mixed and wrestling-style events.

Japan then built its own mixed leagues. Satoru Sayama founded *Shooto* in the mid-1980s. Pancrase held its first event in September 1993, two months before the first UFC. Pride Fighting Championships began in 1997 at the Tokyo Dome. These *promotions*, companies that organize and sell events, grew in Japan alongside the American league.

a Japanese mixed martial arts organization founded by Satoru Sayama in the 1980s

lessons.title: UFC 1 in Denver
lessons.mainIdea: The first Ultimate Fighting Championship was a pay-per-view tournament held in Denver on November 12, 1993.
reading: On November 12, 1993, the first Ultimate Fighting Championship took place at McNichols Sports Arena in Denver, Colorado. It was produced by Semaphore Entertainment Group, a television company. Advertising executive Art Davie and Rorion Gracie, Hélio Gracie's eldest son, helped plan it.

The event was an eight-man *tournament*. Fighters came from different backgrounds, including boxing, karate, sumo and savate. Royce Gracie, Rorion's younger brother, won three bouts in one night. The fights took place inside an eight-sided fenced ring called the *Octagon*. The Octagon became the company's trademark.

The main audience watched on *pay-per-view*, meaning viewers paid a fee to see one event on cable television. Selling each event to home viewers made UFC a television business first. Its early shows were built to answer one question for audiences: which style would win? That question sold tickets, but it was a marketing idea, not a sport with fixed rules.

lessons.title: Style Against Style
lessons.mainIdea: Early UFC shows were advertised as having almost no rules and as a test of styles, and both ideas soon changed.
reading: Early UFC advertising said there were no rules. That was not quite true. The first events banned biting and eye gouging, and a referee stood in the Octagon. Still, there were no *weight classes*, no rounds and no judges. A small fighter could face a much larger one.

The shows pitched each bout as a test between styles, such as karate against wrestling. Within a few years, fighters stopped entering as the champion of one style. They trained in several arts at once. The name *mixed martial arts* came into common use in the 1990s to describe this new training and sport.

Some fans and promoters described the sport as an ancient secret brought back to life. Historians see a *modern invention*, built by television producers, promoters and later government officials. Its roots are in twentieth-century rooms: wrestling mats, boxing gyms, judo halls, Brazilian academies and Thai stadiums. It is not the return of a lost temple art.

words.d: groups that match competitors of similar body weight
a combat sport that allows skills from several arts; often shortened to MMA
something created recently by known people, even if it borrows from older traditions

lessons.title: Calls for a Ban
lessons.mainIdea: In the mid-1990s, political opposition pushed UFC off most cable systems, and new owners bought it in 2001.
reading: In 1996 Senator John McCain of Arizona watched a tape of a UFC event. He called the sport human cockfighting and wrote to state governors, urging them to ban it. McCain was a boxing fan and a leading voice on boxing safety. His campaign gave *opponents* of the sport a national spokesman.

Pressure grew. In 1997 major cable companies stopped carrying UFC pay-per-view shows. New York State passed a law banning professional mixed martial arts that same year. Without cable or big arenas, UFC moved to smaller venues and lost money. Semaphore Entertainment Group began changing its rules to win back *legitimacy*, the public sense that something is proper and lawful.

In January 2001, Zuffa bought UFC for about two million dollars. Zuffa was owned by brothers Frank and Lorenzo Fertitta, casino executives in Las Vegas. Dana White became company president. Their plan was to work with state athletic commissions, not against them. That *strategy* shaped the league that exists today.

lessons.title: What a Commission Does
lessons.mainIdea: State athletic commissions, first built for boxing, license fighters and officials and approve every professional bout.
reading: In the United States, each state decides whether professional combat sports may take place there. Many states use an *athletic commission*, a government board that oversees boxing and similar sports. New York created its State Athletic Commission under the Walker Law of 1920. Nevada created its commission in 1941.

A commission issues licenses to fighters, referees, judges, promoters and seconds. It requires medical exams and runs official weigh-ins before events. It assigns officials to each bout and keeps the results. A *sanction* is the commission's official approval of an event. Without it, a professional bout in that state is not lawful.

Congress passed the Muhammad Ali Boxing Reform Act in 2000. It set national rules on contracts and money in professional boxing. The law covers boxing, not mixed martial arts. So MMA still depends mainly on state commissions. The *Association of Boxing Commissions*, a national group of these state and tribal bodies, helps them share rules.

words.d: a government board that licenses and oversees professional combat sports in a state
official approval from a governing body that allows an event to take place
a national group of U.S. state and tribal commissions that share rules for combat sports

lessons.title: The Unified Rules
lessons.mainIdea: New Jersey wrote a shared MMA rule book in 2000 and 2001, and commissions nationwide adopted it by 2009.
reading: In 2000 and 2001, the New Jersey State Athletic Control Board met with promoters and officials to write rules for mixed martial arts. The result became known as the *Unified Rules of Mixed Martial Arts*. In 2001 Nevada's commission also began sanctioning MMA. UFC 33, held in Las Vegas in September 2001, ran under Nevada's approval.

The rules set weight classes, like those in boxing and wrestling. Regular bouts have three rounds of five minutes, and championship bouts have five. Fighters wear light gloves and mouthguards. The rules list a long set of fouls, and three judges score each round. A *ten-point must system*, borrowed from boxing, gives the round winner ten points.

In 2009 the Association of Boxing Commissions adopted the Unified Rules as the national model. State commissions still decide for themselves, but most follow this shared book. The ABC has revised the rules since then. The rule book turned a show into a *regulated* sport, one that follows written rules enforced by an authority.

lessons.title: New York's Long Ban
lessons.mainIdea: New York banned professional MMA from 1997 until a 2016 law, and UFC 205 at Madison Square Garden followed that year.
reading: New York's 1997 law made professional mixed martial arts illegal in the state. As other states sanctioned the sport in the 2000s, New York held out. Amateur events and fans kept the question alive. Each year, bills to lift the ban were introduced in the state *legislature*, the body that makes state laws.

The State Senate passed bills several times, but the Assembly did not bring one to a vote for years. Supporters pointed to jobs, tax money and the Unified Rules. Opponents raised concerns about injuries and brain health. In 2016 the Assembly finally voted yes. Governor Andrew Cuomo signed the law that April, and the *repeal* took effect later that year.

On November 12, 2016, UFC 205 was held at Madison Square Garden in New York City. It came twenty-three years to the day after UFC 1 in Denver. The New York State Athletic Commission, formed under the Walker Law, now oversaw MMA too. New York had been the last state with a ban on professional MMA. Its repeal marked the sport's legal *acceptance* across the country.

the cancelling of a law by a new law
being approved or allowed by people or by law

lessons.title: Rooms MMA Borrowed
lessons.mainIdea: MMA took its training and many of its athletes from older institutions: wrestling mats, boxing gyms, judo clubs, Thai stadiums and sambo halls.
reading: Many early MMA champions came from college wrestling. The NCAA has run national wrestling championships since 1928. Mark Coleman, Dan Severn and Randy Couture all wrestled at a high level before MMA. The sport's weigh-ins and weight classes echo those of the *amateur* wrestling world, where athletes are not paid.

From boxing, MMA took the ring officials, judges, round lengths, gloves and the state commission itself. From Thailand came *Muay Thai*, the national combat sport of Thailand. Its best-known venues are Bangkok's Rajadamnern Stadium, opened in 1945, and Lumpinee Stadium, opened in 1956. Thai trainers began teaching in gyms abroad.

Judo, an Olympic sport since 1964, sent many athletes to MMA. *Sambo* was recognized as a sport by the Soviet All-Union Sports Committee in 1938. Russian sambo champions such as Fedor Emelianenko became MMA stars in Japan's Pride. Each of these rooms has its own rule book and governing body. MMA borrowed from all of them.

lessons.title: Women in the Octagon
lessons.mainIdea: Ronda Rousey, an Olympic judo medalist, and Liz Carmouche fought the first women's bout in UFC history in 2013.
reading: For its first twenty years, UFC held no women's bouts. Other promotions did. Strikeforce and smaller groups in the 2000s featured women fighters such as Gina Carano. Promoters in Japan held women's events as well. The UFC's leaders said for years that they did not plan a *women's division*.

Ronda Rousey changed that plan. She won a bronze medal in judo at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. She was the first American woman to win an Olympic medal in judo. Her mother, AnnMaria De Mars, had won the world judo championship in 1984, the first American to do so. Rousey moved to MMA and became Strikeforce's champion in 2012.

On February 23, 2013, Rousey faced Liz Carmouche at UFC 157 in Anaheim, California. Carmouche, a U.S. Marine veteran, was also the first openly gay fighter in the UFC. Rousey won. The bout made women's MMA a permanent part of the league. It shows a pattern seen across sport: doors opened when a *pioneer*, the first to do something, proved audiences would come.

lessons.title: A League With Owners
lessons.mainIdea: Unlike Olympic sports run by federations, the UFC is a private company, bought and sold as a business, whose events still answer to state law.
reading: In January 2005, the reality show The Ultimate Fighter began on Spike TV. Young fighters lived together and competed for a UFC contract. The show's first finale in April 2005 drew a large cable audience. In 2011 UFC signed a broadcast deal with Fox. Television made UFC the largest *league* in the sport.

In July 2016, Zuffa sold UFC to a group led by WME-IMG, later called Endeavor, for about four billion dollars. In 2023 UFC merged with the professional wrestling company WWE to form TKO Group Holdings. These sales show that UFC is a private business. Its owners set its schedule, its rankings and its pay, subject to the law.

Olympic sports are different. Judo has the International Judo Federation, and wrestling has United World Wrestling. A *federation* is a group of national bodies that writes one set of rules for a sport. Professional MMA has no single federation that owns it. Illinois shows how the pieces fit: UFC 90 was held at the Allstate Arena in Rosemont in October 2008, under Illinois state *licensing*.

review.q: Why is it accurate to call the UFC a league rather than a federation?
choices: It sends teams to the Olympics
It is run by national sports bodies
It is a private company that runs events for profit
review.why: The UFC is a privately owned business; a federation is made of national bodies.
